newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Cholera said threatening 250,000 refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Cholera said threatening 250,000 refugees in Zaire.

text.p: Cholera has broken out at a hillside settlement of about 250,000 Rwanda Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire and could wipe out many within days, a doctor said on Tuesday.

Walter Bonifazio, a doctor with the U.N.-funded agency Doctors in Catastrophic Situations, told Reuters the refugees were trapped in the village of Mwenga, 200 km (120 miles) west of rebel-held Bukavu in east Zaire's border region.
More than a million Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees fled their camps when fighting broke out between Zairean troops and Tutsi rebels a month ago. The whereabouts of many have been a mystery.

"Cholera broke out at Mwenga on Saturday night, but there is also dysentery and malnutrition. This, put together with the conditions of the 250,000 people, is like putting fuel on fire," Bonifazio said in the Rwandan capital Kigali.
"The human loss will be impossible to calculate, it is a bomb, a very big bomb, and the people will die like flies unless help reaches them soon," he added.
He said the 250,000 people at Mwenga were hostages of heavily armed former Rwandan Hutu militia and of soldiers of Rwanda's ousted Hutu army and Zairean troops.
Bonifazio was evacuated from Bukavu at the end of October and said his information was based on radio reports reaching his expatriate colleagues who are still working at Bukavu hospital.
He said he believed several people had already died, but he had no exact figures.
Up to 400,000 refugees are believed to be without any aid in Mugunga refugee camp, further north near the border town of Goma.

Cholera killed at least 30,000 refugees within weeks after more than one million Hutus fled from Rwanda into eastern Zaire in 1994 after the genocide by Hutu extremists of up to a million Tutsis and other victims.
Aid workers say thousands of refugees have already died in rough terrain across eastern Zaire and even if a U.N. force to bring aid came today, many more would be too sick to save.
The aid agency Medecins Sans Frontieres (Doctors without Frontiers) said on Tuesday they estimated some 1,000 were dying every day, based on their experience from working in crises around the globe.

Cholera can cause rapid dehydration and death within hours. Cholera bacteria breed in lakes and are spread by the flies that multiply in corpses, which few people will have the energy or means to bury in the region's thin, patchy soil.
